name: Abdeel
title: Father of Shelemiah
summary: Abdeel is a person known exclusively from the book of Jeremiah as the father of Shelemiah. His son was one of three court officials whom King Jehoiakim sent to arrest the prophet Jeremiah and the scribe Baruch after the king, in anger, had burned the scroll containing Jeremiah's prophecies (Jer 36:26). Abdeel himself does not play an active role in the narrative, but the fact that his name is preserved as a patronym suggests that his family likely held an official position at the court in Jerusalem. The event took place during a critical period around 605–604 BC, when the power of the Neo-Babylonian Empire was growing rapidly under Nebuchadnezzar. The name Abdeel means 'servant of God' in Hebrew, a designation that testifies to religious devotion within the naming tradition.

keyEvents.title: Shelemiah sent to arrest Jeremiah and Baruch
keyEvents.description: After Jeremiah's prophecies were written on a scroll by the scribe Baruch and read aloud to King Jehoiakim, the king reacted by cutting up the scroll and throwing it into the fire. Then the king ordered Shelemiah, son of Abdeel, along with Jerahmeel and Seraiah, to arrest the prophet Jeremiah and the scribe Baruch. However, the Lord hid both of them so that they could not be found.

footnotes.text: The name Abdeel (Hebrew: עַבְדְּאֵל, 'Avd'el') means 'servant of God' or 'God's servant'. It is composed of 'eved' (servant) and 'El' (God), a common naming pattern in Semitic languages that reflects piety and devotion to God. Similar name forms are found in other Northwest Semitic inscriptions.

Abdeel is mentioned only in Jer 36:26, where his son Shelemiah is one of three men King Jehoiakim sends to arrest Jeremiah and Baruch. The fact that he is named as a patronym may suggest that the family held some status or official position at the court in Jerusalem.

The event of the burning of the scroll is dated to the fourth or fifth year of Jehoiakim's reign (c. 605–604 BC), a very turbulent period when Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar was becoming the dominant power in the Middle East after its victory at Carchemish.

In rabbinic tradition, Abdeel himself receives little attention, but the episode where King Jehoiakim burns the scroll (Jer 36) has become an important example of resistance against God's word and prophetic authority. Jehoiakim's actions are seen as an expression of pride that ultimately leads to judgment upon him and his dynasty.

Archaeological finds from the period, including the Lachish letters and seal impressions (bullae) from Jerusalem, confirm the existence of a complex bureaucracy at the court in the last century of the Kingdom of Judah's existence. Court officials with official missions, such as Shelemiah, fit well into this picture.
